en.body:
## From All-American to Marine Corps Grit

Peter Berg, a director known for his unflinching portrayals of American heroism and struggle, returns with **The Mosquito Bowl**. This historical drama, based on Buzz Bissinger's narrative non-fiction, chronicles the lives of four elite college football players who answered the call of duty following the attack on Pearl Harbor. In the early 1940s, a golden era for college football, stars like **John McLaughry**, **Bob Bauman**, **Tony Butkovich**, and **Dave Schreiner** were at the pinnacle of their sport, celebrated as All-Americans and team captains. Butkovich, nicknamed "Touchdown Tony," was even a first-round NFL draft pick. Their promising futures, filled with adoration and ambition, were irrevocably altered by the events of December 1941, prompting them to enlist in the United States Marine Corps.

The film, co-written by **Mark L. Smith** (known for his work on Berg's **American Primeval** and **The Boys in the Boat**), immerses viewers in the visceral realities of World War II. The transition from the celebrated world of college football to the unforgiving battlefields of the Pacific, including the brutal invasion of Okinawa, is stark. Berg emphasizes the core themes of hard work and the importance of believing in something larger than oneself. While the ensemble features notable talents like **Bill Skarsgård** as Bob Bauman and **Nicholas Galitzine**, it's **Ray Nicholson** as Tony Butkovich who emerges as the film's emotional anchor, grounding the narrative with a performance marked by realism and faithfulness to the young men's true stories.

## The Heart of the Game and the War

**The Mosquito Bowl** attempts to capture the essence of a pivotal moment in history through the lens of these extraordinary young athletes. Their decision to set aside personal glory for national service highlights a profound sense of duty and sacrifice. The film’s strength lies in its exploration of this duality – the dreams of athletic greatness juxtaposed with the grim realities of war. For fans of Berg's previous works like **Lone Survivor** and **Patriot's Day**, this film offers a similar blend of intense action and character-driven drama, focusing on the human cost of conflict. The narrative arc follows these men from the roar of the stadium crowd to the deafening sounds of battle, showcasing their resilience and camaraderie under extreme pressure.

## What's Next

As **The Mosquito Bowl** makes its debut, audiences can anticipate a powerful exploration of courage and sacrifice. Further details regarding its availability on streaming platforms beyond Netflix are yet to be announced, but the film is poised to resonate with viewers who appreciate historical dramas that honor the bravery of those who served.

Kane Skennar/Netflix ©2026 Based on the narrative non-fiction book The Mosquito Bowl: A Game of Life and Death in World War II from Pulitzer Prize-winning author Buzz Bissinger, The Mosquito Bowl is the latest historical drama from co-writer/producer/director Peter Berg ( Lone Survivor , Patriot’s Day ) that follows the lives of 4 standout college football players as they answer the call of duty to join the United States Marine Corps during World War II after the bombing of Pearl Harbor. The film adaptation is co-written by veteran screenwriter Mark L. Smith, who worked alongside Berg on his Netflix series American Primeval and has penned a recent historical sports-inspired drama with his script for the Depression-era Olympic rowing team story The Boys in the Boat . Set in the first half of the 1940s, the film drops us into the “leatherhead” era of college football, an era that saw the highest popularity for the sport. 4 players – John McLaughry, Bob Bauman, Tony Butkovich, and Dave Schreiner – are on top of the college football world; breaking records, becoming All-Americans, and leading their men as captains of major college programs such as Wisconsin and Brown. Touchdown Tony Butkovich, in particular, had just been drafted in the first round into the NFL by the Cleveland Rams. Adored by fans as well as their best girls and loving families, these young men had the whole world ahead of them just as the Japanese bombed Pearl Harbor in December 1941. With everything to lose, these young men put all their ambitions aside as they enlist into the Marine Corps to be ultimately sent to Japan ahead of some of the bloodiest, most brutal battles of the war including the invasion of Okinawa. The film starts with a quote from President Herbert Hoover that reads: “Older Men declare war but it is youth that must fight and die and it is youth who must inherit the tribulation, the sorrow, and the triumphs.” Setting a tone that forces its audience to live in the impact of war and sit in the sheer unease of government decisions to change the lives of young men forever, Berg’s film adaptation follows quite closely to the spirit of Bissinger’s book; a book that ends every chapter with a list of soldiers who lost their lives during World War II. Watch the trailer   Berg, whose father was a Marine in the Korean War, explained as much during the Q&A following the opening night theatrical premiere: “We made this film to remind people (of) the cost of war.
